name: Jessner peel

lead: The Jessner peel is a light chemical peel made from resorcinol, salicylic acid and lactic acid. It is used for pigment, acne and texture concerns and sometimes as a first layer before a deeper TCA peel.
Research specific to it is limited to small comparative studies, for example in melasma.

paras: The acids cause controlled superficial injury, after which the outer skin layers shed and renew.
Reported effects of peels include stinging, redness, dryness, photosensitivity and, less often, pigment change or scarring.

lead: The Jessner peel is a superficial chemical peel based on Jessner's solution, a mixture of resorcinol, salicylic acid and lactic acid. Chemical peels are procedures in which an acid or other agent is applied to the skin to cause controlled injury, after which the skin sheds and renews itself; the general category is described as being used for fine lines, acne scarring and uneven pigmentation.[1] Retinoic acid peels are described as commonly being preceded by a Jessner peel.[1]

In dermatology literature the Jessner solution is also used as a pre-treatment step before a medium-depth trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel, a combination known as the Jessner's + TCA peel. Authors of a 2017 paper on TCA technique noted that physicians often choose lighter peels, such as glycolic acid or Jessner peels, and various lasers for patients with darker skin out of concern about pigmentary complications from deeper peels.[2]

Published human research specific to the Jessner peel is limited. A 2021 comparative study in Indian women with melasma compared a 35% glycolic acid peel with a Jessner peel as add-ons to a triple topical combination.[3]

paras: The Jessner peel is generally classed among light-depth chemical peels. Light peels, as a group, are described as treating fine wrinkles, uneven pigmentation and acne, with side effects including stinging, redness, irritation and dryness.[1] Salicylic acid, one of its components, is a beta hydroxy acid described as oil-soluble and used in acne treatment.[1]

In some medium-depth protocols, a Jessner application is used first and TCA applied afterwards. A 1989 report described this Jessner's + TCA approach as a medium-depth peel used for photoaged skin, actinic keratoses and wrinkles.

Chemical peels in general are associated with photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, and in some cases scarring; deeper peels carry more risk.[1] Concern about pigmentary complications in darker skin is the reason some clinicians reported favouring lighter peels such as the Jessner peel over deeper ones.[2]

A 2021 study from Baroda Medical College, India, enrolled 60 women with melasma and compared a 35% glycolic acid peel with a Jessner peel, each added to a triple combination cream of hydroquinone, tretinoin and fluocinolone acetonide.[3] A later registered trial listed on ClinicalTrials.gov compared Jessner's solution with TCA for melasma in 19 participants (completed, Phase 4, start 2008). Jessner's solution has also been studied as a priming step in combination with TCA in the 1989 and 1995 dermatology papers.
The Jessner peel is listed in the wiki as a skin-resurfacing procedure within the hardmaxxing category. No forum material on it was collected for this entry.

timeline.event: The Jessner's + TCA medium-depth peel is described in a dermatologic surgery journal.
A further review of the Jessner's-TCA peel appears in Dermatologic Clinics.
